graph_authoring_scope.aspect_name: Statistical learning and linear regression foundations
graph_authoring_scope.aspect_description: Diagnosable concepts from ISLP Chapter 2 sections 2.1-2.2 and Chapter 3 sections 3.1-3.5: statistical-learning objectives, model assessment, flexibility and generalization, and simple and multiple linear-regression formulation, inference, and diagnosis.
representative_tasks: Identify predictors, response, the unknown function, and the error term in a new statistical-learning scenario.
Explain the difference between predicting an outcome and inferring how predictors relate to the outcome.
Separate reducible error from irreducible error and explain which component modeling can address.
Decide whether a stated scientific goal calls primarily for prediction, inference, or both.
Compare parametric and non-parametric approaches in terms of assumptions, flexibility, and data requirements.
Explain how a two-stage parametric method first assumes a functional form and then estimates parameters.
Diagnose underfitting and overfitting from training and test performance.
Explain why lower training error does not guarantee better test performance.
Relate model flexibility to interpretability without claiming that one is always preferable.
Choose an appropriate flexibility level for a small noisy data set and justify the trade-off.
Distinguish supervised learning from unsupervised learning using the availability and role of a response variable.
Distinguish regression from classification by the nature of the response rather than the algorithm name.
Select a loss measure appropriate for a quantitative-response prediction problem.
Compute and interpret mean squared error on training data and on held-out test data.
Explain why test error is the relevant quantity for generalization even when only training data are used to fit the model.
Describe the typical U-shaped relationship between flexibility and expected test error.
Decompose expected test error conceptually into variance, squared bias, and irreducible error.
Predict how increasing flexibility generally affects bias and variance.
Explain why the lowest achievable test error can remain positive even for the true function.
Use the bias-variance trade-off to compare two candidate models with different complexity.
Explain the role of K-nearest neighbors as a flexible method without treating its local averaging rule as linear regression.
Predict how changing K in K-nearest neighbors affects flexibility, bias, and variance.
Explain the population linear-regression model and distinguish its coefficients from their sample estimates.
Interpret the intercept and slope in a simple linear regression within the units and support of the data.
Write the least-squares objective for simple linear regression and explain what it minimizes.
Distinguish a residual from the unobserved error term in the population model.
Use a fitted regression equation to make a prediction and state the limits of extrapolation.
Explain what the residual standard error estimates and what a large value implies.
Interpret R-squared as a proportion of response variability explained by the fitted linear model.
Explain why a high R-squared does not by itself establish causation or good out-of-sample performance.
Distinguish correlation from R-squared in simple linear regression and explain their relationship.
Formulate a multiple linear-regression model with several predictors.
Interpret one multiple-regression coefficient while holding the other included predictors fixed.
Explain why separate simple regressions can disagree with one multiple regression when predictors are correlated.
Use an F-test question to distinguish evidence for at least one association from evidence about a specific predictor.
State the null and alternative hypotheses for testing one regression coefficient.
Interpret a standard error and confidence interval for a regression coefficient.
Explain what a small p-value does and does not establish in a regression analysis.
Distinguish a confidence interval for a mean response from a prediction interval for a new observation.
Explain why a prediction interval is wider than a confidence interval at the same predictor values.
Diagnose non-linearity from a residual plot and state why a linear term may be inadequate.
Diagnose heteroscedasticity from residual behavior and explain which model assumption it challenges.
Identify a potential outlier using residual information without confusing it with high leverage.
Identify a high-leverage observation from unusual predictor values and explain its possible influence.
Explain how an influential observation combines residual size and leverage.
Diagnose collinearity and explain why it inflates uncertainty in individual coefficient estimates.
Distinguish interaction effects from additive effects in a regression model.
Interpret an interaction coefficient by explaining how one predictor changes the effect of another.
Represent a qualitative predictor with indicator variables while identifying the reference category.
Critique a regression conclusion by checking objective, assumptions, diagnostics, uncertainty, and generalization evidence together.
excluded_topics: Python lab procedures, package APIs, and environment setup
End-of-chapter coding exercises and dataset-specific implementation details
Classification methods beyond the Chapter 2 regression-versus-classification distinction
Resampling, cross-validation, and bootstrap methods from later chapters
Regularization, subset selection, and dimension reduction
Nonlinear regression methods beyond diagnosing non-linearity
Tree methods, support vector machines, deep learning, survival analysis, and unsupervised learning
Formal matrix derivations and proof-oriented asymptotic theory
Causal claims not supported by the selected chapters
Advanced model-selection criteria not developed in the selected scope
